units.title: Ranking four angles fast
units.subtitle: Find the extremes, decide the middle pair, ignore the arms.

blocks.title: Compare pairs, not the whole set
blocks.text: An angle-ranking item shows four angles numbered 1 to 4 and asks for their order from smallest to largest; the answer options are orderings such as 2-1-4-3. Do not try to rank all four at once. Scan for the angle that is clearly the smallest and the one that is clearly the largest, because those two are usually obvious and they eliminate most of the options immediately. What remains is almost always a decision between two middle angles that are close in size, and the surviving options typically share the same first and last entries and differ only in the middle. That is the comparison the item is really testing, so spend your remaining seconds there and nowhere else.

blocks.title: Anchor to 90 and 180 degrees
blocks.text: Your eye judges an angle far better against a reference than in isolation. For each angle ask whether it is smaller than a right angle, close to one, or wider, and for very wide angles ask how far it falls short of a straight line. Two angles that sit on opposite sides of 90 degrees are already ranked. When two angles are on the same side, imagine both rotated so that one arm is horizontal and compare the height the other arm reaches at the same distance from the vertex; a small gap in height means a small gap in angle. Very small angles are easier to compare by the gap between the arms at their tips than by the arms themselves.

blocks.title: Arm length and orientation are distractions
blocks.text: An angle is an opening, not a pair of lines. Unequal arm lengths distort the comparison even though the measure has not changed, so compare only the region where both arms exist. An angle that opens downward or to the left also reads differently from one that opens upward, and item writers rotate angles for exactly that reason. The fix is mechanical: picture both arms trimmed to the same short length from the vertex, then compare the gap between the tips. Budget about twenty to twenty-five seconds for each item, never try to measure, and once the middle pair is decided, commit and move on; revisiting angles costs time that the later subtests need more.

example.prompt: Four angles are shown. Angle 3 is clearly the widest and angle 2 clearly the narrowest, and two options begin with 2 and end with 3: 2-1-4-3 and 2-4-1-3. How do you decide?
example.reasoning: The extremes have done their work by eliminating the other options, so the only question left is whether angle 1 or angle 4 is smaller. Picture both with equal arm lengths and compare each to a right angle; the one that falls further short is smaller and goes second.

units.prediction: Predict which of two angles of equal measure will look larger when one is drawn with arms twice as long, and what happens to that impression when you imagine the long arms trimmed.

questions.stem: Two angles have the same measure, but one is drawn with arms twice as long. Compared with the short-armed angle, the long-armed angle:
options: Is larger, because its arms enclose more area
Has the same measure; arm length does not change an angle
Is smaller, because its arms diverge more slowly
Cannot be compared until the arms are redrawn equal
questions.explanation: An angle is the opening between two rays, and extending the rays changes nothing about that opening. The enclosed-area argument is the trap: the region between longer arms is bigger, but area is not what an angle measures.

questions.stem: Four angles must be ranked from smallest to largest. Which first step saves the most time?
options: Estimate each angle in degrees to the nearest five
Compare angles 1 and 2, then 2 and 3, then 3 and 4 in order
Rotate the page so that every angle opens upward
Identify the clearly smallest and clearly largest, then decide the middle pair
questions.explanation: The extremes are usually obvious and eliminate most options at once, leaving one pairwise decision. Estimating degrees is the trap: it feels rigorous but costs far more than the item’s time budget and is no more accurate than a direct comparison.

questions.stem: An angle opens slightly wider than the corner of a square. Its measure is best described as:
options: Slightly more than 90 degrees
Slightly less than 90 degrees
Close to 180 degrees
Close to 45 degrees
questions.explanation: The corner of a square is a right angle, so an opening just wider than it is just over 90 degrees. Anchoring to the square is exactly the reference habit the method relies on; the slightly-less option is the reversal trap.

questions.stem: After you eliminate the others, the two remaining ranking options share the same first and last angles and differ only in the middle two. What does this tell you?
options: One of the two options is a misprint
The extremes are wrong and should be re-checked
The middle pair is the decision the item is really testing
The two middle angles are equal in measure
questions.explanation: Once only these two remain, the extremes no longer separate them, so the middle pair is the one comparison still open and deserves all the remaining attention. Re-checking the extremes is the trap: it re-does work that cannot change which of the two survivors you pick.

questions.stem: Two angles, one opening to the upper left and one opening downward, look different in size. What is the reliable way to compare them?
options: Compare the lengths of their arms
Picture both rotated so that one arm is horizontal, then compare the openings
Assume the downward one is larger, because it looks heavier
Count how much empty space surrounds each one
questions.explanation: Orientation changes how an angle reads, not what it measures, so mentally rotating both to a common orientation removes the distraction. Comparing arm lengths is the trap: arm length is the other distraction the item writer controls, and it says nothing about the angle.

questions.stem: An angle appears to measure about 170 degrees. Which reference is most useful for confirming its size?
options: A 45-degree angle
A right angle
A 60-degree angle
A straight line of 180 degrees
questions.explanation: A very wide angle is judged by how far it falls short of a straight line, so 180 degrees is the natural anchor. A right angle is the trap because it is the usual reference, but 170 degrees is so far past 90 that the comparison gives no useful resolution.
